transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-10
Start: 10:00 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Samir Gupta (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood CSM); Maya Chen (BrightHealth AI ML Lead), David Ortiz (Infra), Leah Summers (Product)

Summary:
Quick weekly sync for the POC focused on caching (prefix + KV). Reviewed current metrics, talked through improvements (normalization, TTLs, dedupe), and planned a staging stress test. Agreed next steps and owners.

Topics:
- Current prefix cache hit rates and KV cache hit rates
- Prompt reuse strategy and normalization
- Seeding strategy and eviction/TTL tuning
- Security/data residency concerns for cached payloads
- Benchmarks and staging tests on Dedicated nodes

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: All right everyone, thanks for joining. uh let's kick off, quick agenda — hit rates, tuning, next steps. Maya, can you start with what you saw this week?
[00:18] Maya Chen: Yeah, thanks. so our numbers, um prefix cache overall is low right now, around 18% if you look at the baseline, and KV cache hit is about 42% for the conversational flows. there's big variance by route.
[00:36] Samir Gupta: Got it. is that 42% measured after normalization? like are you normalizing whitespace/IDs?
[00:45] Maya Chen: not aggressively. currently the traffic is basically raw user prompts — we do light trimming, but no canonicalization. so I think a chunk of missed prefixes are due to small variations, tokens like patient IDs, timestamps, basically dynamic bits.
[01:02] Jordan Lee: okay that aligns with what we expected. so two levers: one is prefix normalization / token masking on client side before hitting cache; two is improving prefix seeding — capture common templates.
[01:16] Leah Summers: when you say prefix, do you mean the initial N tokens, right? like the first 50 tokens? we've been using a 64-token prefix window in our baseline.
[01:27] Samir Gupta: yeah, in our instrumentation we use 64 tokens by default for this workload. but we can tune down to 32 for faster matches and less KV size. tradeoff is potentially lower semantic context.
[01:40] David Ortiz: curious about memory — if we increase seeding to store more variants won't that blow up the KV store size? we have quotas on the Dedicated node.
[01:50] Jordan Lee: right — that's why seeding focuses on top-k templates only. we also do TTL based eviction. current suggestions are: seed top 500 templates, normalize before seed, set TTL to 6 hours for route-level caches during peak, and 24 hours for stable templates.
[02:07] Maya Chen: can you explain the difference between prefix cache and KV cache again — I know but want to be clear for the rest of the team.
[02:13] Samir Gupta: sure — prefix cache is usually a short hash of the prompt prefix that lets the runtime skip the first N tokens; KV cache is the model's key-value attention cache you persist to reuse for same conversation state across requests. They complement each other: prefix cache avoids re-encoding tokens, KV provides faster decode by reusing past attention state.
[02:33] Maya Chen: okay makes sense. so our prefix hit is 18%, KV is 42%, is that normal?
[02:38] Samir Gupta: for un-normalized, template-heavy workloads that's within expected. with normalization and seeding we typically see prefix hit climb into 40–60% range and KV up to 60–70% depending on prompt reuse.
[02:50] Leah Summers: what about dedupe? we have a small subset of prompts that are essentially the same but differ by patient name or ID — can we mask those?
[02:58] Samir Gupta: absolutely. we recommend parameterizing PII and stable fields. Samir: sorry, Samir here, we can provide a sample script — prefix normalization sample — to run as a preprocess.
[03:08] Maya Chen: perfect. do you have examples of regex/tokenization approaches?
[03:13] Samir Gupta: yes, we'll share a normalization doc. in short: strip PII like emails/ids, replace numeric tokens with <NUM>, dates with <DATE>, and do whitespace normalization. also lowercasing might help depending on prompt semantics.
[03:28] Jordan Lee: quick note on correctness: any normalization has to preserve semantics. for clinical prompts, don't mask clinical signs. focus on extraneous noise.
[03:36] David Ortiz: security question — if we cache prompts with patient info, is there an encryption or key management concern? do we store sensitive fields?
[03:44] Priya Nair: good point. Redwood's policy for private deployments: by default, customer-managed KMS can be used to encrypt KV snapshots at rest, and we can configure redaction hooks to avoid storing raw PII in caches. For hosted tests we recommend redaction.
[03:58] Leah Summers: so for the POC we're on a staging Dedicated node, correct? are the caches encrypted?
[04:04] Jordan Lee: yes staging Dedicated with customer VPC. Samir, correct me if wrong — we enabled KMS at rest encryption and configured cache redaction for any fields the customer flags.
[04:12] Samir Gupta: that's right — and David, for the stress test we can keep full encryption enabled. we'll provide a config you can audit before the run.
[04:20] Maya Chen: on benchmarks — Jordan you sent last week's numbers; what changed since then?
[04:26] Jordan Lee: we rolled an updated seeding job and small normalization. prefix moved 18% -> 27%, KV 42% -> 49% over 48 hours. but there was a regression on tail latency for some longer sequences because of increased cache lookup overhead; we have a patch to reduce lookup contention.
[04:43] David Ortiz: tail latency regression — can you quantify p95/p99?
[04:47] Jordan Lee: p95 unchanged (~220ms), p99 increased from 720ms to 1.05s on some routes. Samir has a mitigation: async lookups + opportunistic fallbacks.
[04:59] Samir Gupta: Yes — we can make cache reads asynchronous up to a timeout, and if no hit we proceed with normal encode path. That reduces blocking on cache hits and improves p99. We'll try it in staging.
[05:10] Maya Chen: sounds promising. will that change cost profile? async lookups might slightly increase compute but reduce wasted re-encoding.
[05:18] Samir Gupta: net effect typically lowers token cost because successful hits avoid decode work. unsuccessful async reads add minimal overhead. We'll quantify in the 24h benchmark.
[05:27] Leah Summers: for prefix window — you mentioned reducing to 32 tokens. how does that affect hit semantics?
[05:33] Samir Gupta: shorter window increases exact-match hit rate for templated prompts but may miss context in longer prompts. For BrightHealth flows where templates are short, 32 is often sufficient. We'll compare both in benchmarks.
[05:44] Jordan Lee: action: we'll run A/B 32 vs 64 prefix windows on staging. include cost delta, hit rate, and quality regression checks on our eval set.
[05:54] Maya Chen: for quality checks, we need to be sure clinical intent isn't degraded. we'll provide a small eval set for that.
[06:00] David Ortiz: on provisioning — I can spin up a staging Dedicated node but need the instance profile and storage requirements. what's the KV storage per request estimate?
[06:09] Samir Gupta: ballpark: with 64-token prefix and typical Llama2-like model, KV per active convo is ~150KB. For seeded templates the size depends on how many prefixes you store; seeding 500 templates is modest — under a few GB. We'll send a sizing doc.
[06:23] Maya Chen: good. any risks around cache consistency if we do partial updates during rollout?
[06:30] Jordan Lee: we use versioned keys and can flush per-route. rollout strategy: canary seed first 10%, observe hit rates and errors, then full rollout.
[06:40] Leah Summers: timeline — can we get the benchmark by Thursday?
[06:43] Jordan Lee: yes we can run 24h starting tomorrow and should have results by Thursday EOD.
[06:49] Maya Chen: perfect. do you need more sample traffic?
[06:52] Jordan Lee: yes, top-100 prefixes to prioritize seeding. Maya?
[06:55] Maya Chen: we'll extract and share that today.
[06:58] Priya Nair: I'll attach the security checklist and the KMS config docs to the thread.
[07:02] Jordan Lee: great. recap of next steps and owners...

- Jordan: run 24h benchmark with new seeding + normalization, async cache reads, 32 vs 64 window A/B (deliver results by 2026-11-12)
